column11: ANCHOR, the measured anti-amyloid class new-start rate from CMS Part B beneficiaries. Leqembi (J0174): 961 in 2023 and 7,907 in 2024 (Medicare Part B Spending by Drug, dataset 76a714ad-3a2c-43ac-b76d-9dadf8f7d890) and 14,029 in 2025 (quarterly file bf6a5b3b-31ee-4abb-b1ad-2607a1e7510a, row '2025 (Q1-Q4)'). Kisunla (J0175): 1,299 in 2024 (drug_demand) and 9,993 in 2025 (quarterly file). At this seed's stopping of 0.6866, 31.34% of a year's patients carry into the next, so 2025 new starts are 14,029 - 7,907 x 0.3134 = 11,551 and 9,993 - 1,299 x 0.3134 = 9,586, 21,136 together. In the engine's own terms a year's eligible pool is the carried pool plus the inflow, which in the first year is 2,197,800 + 270,270 = 2,468,070, so the class started 0.8564% of it in 2025. MULTIPLE 0.5, A JUDGEMENT: 0.5 x 0.8564% = 0.4282%, about 10,570 US starts a year on that pool. The engine grows this pool by the inflow with no exit, as it does trontinemab's (see the header), so the same share gives about 13,700 US starts in 2036 and 23,300 in 2045, when exclusivity ends: the checker's global starts of 27,050 and 45,941 over the 1.973 ex-US scaling. Cross-check: Kisunla alone, the second entrant, started 9,586 in its first full year, 45.4% of the class
column12: the 0.5 is a judgement and the most arguable figure here. For more: a different target from every marketed antibody, so it could be added to anti-amyloid therapy rather than replace it, and Fast Track (BMS, 2025-10-01). Against: no efficacy data exist yet and the Phase 2 primary outcome is tau PET, not a clinical scale; N-terminal anti-tau antibodies (gosuranemab, semorinemab, tilavonemab) failed; a second monthly infusion on top of anti-amyloid therapy; a launch around 2032 behind trontinemab and subcutaneous antibodies; and BMS sells no Alzheimer's medicine today. The class rate is itself still rising (Q1 2026 alone had 12,876 Leqembi and 10,782 Kisunla beneficiaries), so the anchor is a measured level, not an extrapolated peak
